item.title: How the Claude Code team does code review
item.description:
Source: claude.dev

Top Comment:

This is like one of Google’s infrastructure blog. Google scale things are only relevant and appropriate for them. We had lots of bitter lessons from smaller engineering teams following the process with the justification that “this is how Google does it”.

Similarly, Anthropic can afford to do this because they have virtually unlimited tokens and labs to train models for their specific usecase. The rest of us need code comprehension lest we become dependent on continuous supply of tokens (which is a state these labs badly want to achieve)

So, unless you work at a lab, or have unlimited tokens guaranteed through the life of your company, it would do both the company and you good to continue to read the code and not let these 30k PRs per engineer be the norm.

An excerpt from the article makes my point

> Nobody on the team keeps a complete mental model of Claude Code in their head, and we don't think anyone needs to. When someone wants to understand a part of the codebase, they ask Claude to write an explainer for exactly that slice. It takes minutes and reflects the code as it is today.

item.title: Butlerian Jihad
item.description:
Source: dune.fandom.com

Top Comment:

A couple of things for your consideration:

In the original 6 Frank Herbert novels, it’s not ever truly explained what problems, if any, the thinking machines were actually causing. And given much of the rest of the setting, it could have very easily been a religious movement against a useful technology that got out of hand. Like Space ISIS blowing up Petra, or a “what would happen if the Luddites won” scenario.

The Dune Encyclopedia, which was not written by him but which he said he considered canonical, says the whole thing was incited when an AI doctor flagged a Bene Gesserit’s baby for abortion due to an alleged genetic defect. The Bene Gesserit woman knew it was healthy because of her abilities, and upon investigation it was found that the hospital’s AI had been running a eugenics program. (Or something like that, it’s been forever since I’ve read this stuff.)

In either case, Herbert really implied that humans took the lead on dismantling AI, and there is never any Terminator or Matrix style machine uprising scenario.

item.title: JPEG XL vs. AVIF for web use-cases
item.description:
Source: jakearchibald.com

Top Comment:

The benchmark[1] (HN discussion [2]) I read from about 2.5 years ago came to roughly the opposite conclusion. JPEG XL dominated practically all other image formats on compressed size and encoding time.

Superficially, that benchmark and this one seem to be taking similar measurements. They both measure encoded size versus encoding time versus perceptual quality metrics, although they present the data on plots with different axes. I haven't had the chance to try to reproduce the results of either yet, but I have no reason to doubt either benchmark.

I wonder what accounts for the difference. Maybe the libavif encoder got a lot better in the last 2.5 years. The older benchmark uses libjxl v0.10.0 and libavif v1.0.3, while the newer one uses libjxl v0.12.0 and libavif v1.4.2. Or maybe it's the set of images used. The older benchmarks aggregates results for small test sets of images, while the newer benchmark tests individual images. The newer benchmark does find an image where JPEG XL wins on file size (the weasel), but it still loses on encoding time, whereas in the older benchmark JPEG XL almost always won on both. Or maybe it's the hardware (M3 Pro vs. M4 Pro).

[1]: https://cloudinary.com/blog/jpeg-xl-and-the-pareto-front

[2]: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=39559281

item.title: Show HN: Llmspeed – feel how fast a local LLM runs before you buy the hardware
item.description:
Source: llmspeed.dev

Top Comment:

I feel like these types of benchmarks mostly test what the mainstream tells you is possible and or works. You rarely get to hear the different implementations of inference engines, different types of setups (e.g. hybrid ones or older hardware) and their pros and cons. Also it seems these were tested with very minimal token usage.

Currently on my 9 year old laptop with a GTX 1070 Max-Q 8GB vram, 16 gb ddr4 ram and i7 8750h. I am running a finetuned Qwen 3.5-35B-A3B (Tiel-Coder-35B-A3B-GGUF-MTP) with 4-bit quant on a llamacpp fork (Turboquant) with 131k context at around 16-19 tk/s and 350-500 tk/s prefil using Pi harness. It is amazing for writing scripts and doing medium coding tasks and summarizing text for me. After around 100k context it goes down to 9 tk/s but that is to be expected.

If you ever ask any frontier LLM or these types of benchmarks, they would probably say that the best model I can run on my system is a crappy 9B model or something, which is just completely false. So I really wonder how much more you can pull out from more powerful systems and much better open weight models.
